title: Census clerks come north for a count
summary: Two census clerks ride to Caol mhòr, the first southern office to ask the Moot for its own count of its own people rather than take none, the shire's own maor having told the surveyor-general no clerk had yet gone north.

title: The Moot's figures given to the census clerks
summary: Daniel Frayne gives the visiting clerks the Moot's own count, kept every third year since the room was opened, along with the school and vigil registers, and offers to swear to the figures before a justice if the council should ask it.

title: Frayne's private book notes the asking
summary: Daniel Frayne writes the day's giving into his own private book, judging it worth the keeping that the Moot had, for once, been asked for its figures rather than merely tolerated in the giving of them.

title: A young clerk asks what the two words mean
summary: Walking out of the room into the frost, a junior clerk asks Daniel Frayne whether the minute's two words oblige the south to answer for what it has printed; Frayne tells him a fact set down is not a promise kept, but cannot be unprinted either.

title: Tormod Pinn buried at Muileann chaol
summary: Tormod Pinn, chronicler nine-and-seventy years old, is buried in the small ground behind the Library among every keeper and chronicler the house has kept since Ailean Leabhar; Mòrag nic Coinnich speaks over him that he kept the list honest and struck nothing from it unearned.

title: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's first morning at the desk
summary: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh, chosen from the Library's own senior clerks, tells the house on her first morning as chronicler that she means to change nothing of the desk's hours, only its habit of silence where the record itself keeps none.

title: Beathag's note sent north to Frayne
summary: A Library clerk sends Daniel Frayne a copy of Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's first foot-note, naming the census clerks' reliance on the Moot's own figures; Frayne keeps it in his private book beside the day he gave them, judging her a chronicler the north may trust.

title: Mòrag nic Coinnich calls the shire chests in
summary: Mòrag nic Coinnich sends her own clerks along the roll to bring every shire's record-chest to Muileann chaol, judging a history kept in forty scattered chests no history at all but forty separate hopes of one day being read together.

title: The Seann Tarr keeper meets the clerks at the gate
summary: The shire keeper who burned his own chest at Seann Tarr meets Mòrag's clerks at the gate the next morning, his coat still smelling of the smoke, and repeats to them plainly that the shire's record belongs in the shire.

title: Cathair naomh's chronicle carried south by its own keeper
summary: The eldest daughter of the family that has kept Cathair naomh's town chronicle four generations rides the two carts south herself and unpacks them at Mòrag nic Coinnich's own table, the chronicle begun by her great-grandmother on the back of an unused rent-roll.

title: Seann Toll's copy becomes the pattern
summary: The full transcription Mòrag's clerks make for Seann Toll, bound and set beside the original before either leaves the shire's hall, becomes the pattern every later shire's copy is cut to.

title: Frayne puts the calling-in to the Moot's own room
summary: Reading the notice of the calling-in, Daniel Frayne calls the room at Caol mhòr together and asks it plainly whether the Moot should offer its own books south now that the council has shown a wish to gather every shire's record.

title: The Moot's minute declining to send its books
summary: After an evening's debate, the room's minute at Caol mhòr records no vote by count and no reason beyond two words its clerk sets down at the close of the sitting: *kept north.* No cart of the Moot's own books goes south that year or after.
